analysis.one_liner: Caps punitive damages and limits liability for small businesses and product sellers facing injury lawsuits.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a committee vote in the Senate Judiciary Committee and died when the 107th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would change courtroom rules for lawsuits against small businesses and against retailers, renters, and other sellers of products. Punitive damages against a business with fewer than 25 employees would be allowed only on a higher burden of proof and capped at the lesser of three times the compensatory award or $250,000. Each small-business defendant would pay only its own share of pain-and-suffering damages rather than being held responsible for the whole award. Retailers and other non-manufacturer sellers could be sued for a defective product only if the injured person proved the seller itself was careless, broke its own warranty, or acted intentionally. The bill was referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee, which never acted on it, and it expired when the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Businesses with fewer than 25 employees would face lower and more predictable damages when they lose lawsuits. Retailers, distributors, renters, and lessors of products would largely escape liability for injuries caused by products they did not make, unless the injured person could prove the seller itself was negligent or broke an express warranty. Liability insurers covering these defendants would pay fewer and smaller claims.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Small businesses, product sellers, and insurers

how_it_helps.text: Punitive damages against a small business would require proof by clear and convincing evidence of conduct showing conscious, flagrant indifference to others' safety, and would be capped at the lesser of three times the compensatory award or $250,000, unless the defendant intended the specific harm [S2][S3].

Each small-business defendant would be liable only for the share of noneconomic damages matching its own percentage of responsibility, ending shared responsibility for the full award in those cases [S2][S3].

A product seller that is not the manufacturer would be liable only if the claimant proved the seller failed to exercise reasonable care, made and broke an express warranty, or engaged in intentional wrongdoing, with a fallback holding the seller liable as a manufacturer when the manufacturer cannot be reached or a judgment against it cannot be enforced [S2][S3].

The bill carves out exceptions so its limits would not apply to crimes of violence, terrorism, hate crimes, sexual offenses, civil rights violations, drunk or drugged driving, environmental damage claims, and fraud actions by the government [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Injured people, including consumers hurt by defective products, would bear the cost. They would find it harder to win punitive damages, could collect only a defendant's proportional share of pain-and-suffering damages, and in many cases could no longer hold a retailer or rental company responsible for a dangerous product, with the manufacturer as the remaining target. State laws offering broader remedies would be overridden unless a state opted out.

drawbacks.text: A person seriously injured by a defective product sold by a retailer could recover from that seller only after proving the seller itself was careless, broke an express warranty, or acted intentionally, even when the seller was part of the chain that put the dangerous product in commerce [S2][S3].

The punitive damages cap of the lesser of three times compensatory damages or $250,000, applied by the judge without the jury knowing, could leave victims of egregious but not specifically intended conduct undercompensated relative to what state law would otherwise allow [S3].

The bill would preempt state tort law nationwide, including joint and several liability rules, unless a state enacted a statute electing out, reducing protections state legislatures had set for their own residents [S3].

The small-business definition covers any entity with fewer than 25 full-time employees, including subsidiaries of larger corporations counted with their parent's employees, so some lawsuits involving sizable operations would still fall under the caps [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill offers real benefits to defendants: more predictable exposure, protection from being pulled into lawsuits over products they did not make, and an escape from paying the entire award when mostly at fault by others. But those gains come directly out of the pockets of injured people, who would face higher proof burdens, capped damages, and fewer defendants to recover from, and it would override state laws that currently protect them. The exceptions for violent crime, drunk driving, civil rights violations, and fraud show drafters recognized the caps would otherwise be too harsh; that recognition itself suggests the baseline rules were too broad.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee, which never scheduled action on it, and it died there when the 107th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator McConnell introduced the bill on May 10, 2001, with Senator Lieberman, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on the Judiciary [S1][S3][S5].
Four senators, one Democrat and three Republicans, cosponsored the bill [S4].
The only further actions were the sponsor's introductory remarks on June 28, 2001 and earlier on May 14; the Judiciary Committee never reported the bill and the Senate never voted on it [S5].
The bill expired with the end of the 107th Congress on January 3, 2003, with no vote in either chamber [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died without a vote, injured consumers kept the full remedies available under state law, including broader punitive damages and the ability to sue sellers of defective products, while small businesses and insurers continued to face those claims.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Injured consumers, who kept existing state-law rights

sides.party_line_note: The bill's small sponsor group was bipartisan, one Democrat and three Republicans joining Senator McConnell, but no vote was ever taken, so no party split on the merits is recorded.

industries.note: The bill would cap punitive damages and end shared responsibility for full awards against businesses with fewer than 25 employees, lowering their litigation costs. That gain comes directly from injured people recovering less after being harmed.

industries.industry: Product retailers, distributors, and rental/leasing companies
industries.note: Non-manufacturer sellers could be sued for harm caused by a product only if the claimant proved the seller itself was careless, broke an express warranty, or acted intentionally, largely insulating sellers from product-liability claims based solely on selling a defective product. Consumers injured by those products would lose a deep-pocket defendant unless the manufacturer was reachable and solvent.

Lower and capped punitive awards and proportionate liability would reduce payouts on claims against covered business clients. The savings would accrue to insurers and policyholders rather than to injured claimants.

Higher proof burdens, damage caps, and seller immunity would reduce the number and size of personal-injury and product-liability cases lawyers could bring on behalf of injured clients. Their interest runs with that of the injured people they represent.
